questions.question: A 40 years old woman comes to the clinic complaining of severe, burning pain in her right hand following a chemical spill causing tissue damage at her workplace. Which of the following substances is responsible for her pain?

explanation.text: Based on the above scenario, the patient most likely has a chemical burn. Bradykinin is involved in mediating the chemical nociceptive stimuli experienced by the patient. Chemical Nociceptive stimuli Both TRPA1 and TRPV1 detects chemical stimuli Bradykinin (most painful chemical stimuli)- B1 & B2 receptors (Option D)

Bradykinin is a potent inflammatory mediator that is released during tissue injury and contributes significantly to the sensation of pain Chemical burns can cause the release of bradykinin and other inflammatory mediators, which activate pain pathways. Other chemical mediators: Serotonin- 5HT receptors Histamine- H3/H4 receptors Nerve endings also have Acid-Sensing Ion Channel (ASIC) receptors that detect H+ and cause acid induced pain.

**Dopamine (Option A):** is involved in motor pathway and not sensory Acetylcholine (Option B) is primarily involved in neuromuscular transmission and autonomic nervous system function Serotonin (Option C) is involved in the pain pathway, but is not the primary mediator in chemical nociceptive stimuli

questions.question: The TRPA1 receptors are activated by all of the following nociceptive stimuli except?

explanation.text: Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) is activated by mechanical, cold and chemical stimuli. Types of nociceptive stimuli and their receptors: Nociceptors can be activated by mechanical, chemical or thermal stimuli.

Mechanical Nociceptors: Respond to strong pressure (eg: from sharp objects) The receptors for mechanical stimuli at free nerve ending include:Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) (also for cold and chemical stimuli) (Option A, C & D ruled out) Mechanical stimuli can also release ATP, which acts on purinergic receptors such as P2X and P2Y and cause pain Thermal Nociceptors: Cold detection: TRP Ankyrin 1 - It is sensitive when the temperature is < 17°C and TRP Melastatin 8 - It is sensitive when the temperature is between 8-28°C. Heat detection: TRP Vanilloid 1(also detects acid and chemicals) (Option B ruled out) - Activated when temperature is > 43°C, H+ ions and capsaicin (the active ingredient of chili).

TRPV2/V3/V4 - It is activated when temperature is > 52°C. Chemical Nociceptors: Both TRPA1 and TRPV1 detects chemical stimuli Nerve endings also have Acid-Sensing Ion Channel (ASIC) receptors that detect H+ and cause acid induced pain Bradykinin (most painful chemical stimuli) - B1 & B2 receptors Serotonin - 5HT receptors Histamine - H3/H4 receptors

questions.question: Nociceptors have their cell bodies located in which of the following structures?

options.B: Ventral horn of the spinal cord

explanation.text: Nociceptors arise from cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion that send one axon to the periphery and another to the spinal cord or brainstem. Nociceptors (pain receptors) are basically the free nerve endings that detect pain sensations. Location of nociceptors: Arise from cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion that send one axon to the periphery and another to the spinal cord or brainstem (Option A).
Nociceptors activate Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels on nerve endings, which causes the neurons to depolarize and generate action potentials.
**Ventral horn of the spinal cord (Option B):** contains motor neuron cell bodies.
**Lateral geniculate nucleus (Option C):** is part of the thalamus and is involved in visual processing.
**Sympathetic ganglion (Option D):** is part of the autonomic nervous system and does not contain the cell bodies of nociceptors.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily involved in fast pain?

explanation.text: Nociceptors: These are responsible for detection of pain. These receptors are basically free nerve endings.

There are two types of pain: Fast pain (First Pain) Slow pain (Second Pain) Fiber Type Aδ fiber Myelinated Large diameter (2-5 µm) C fiber Unmyelinated Smaller diameter (0.4 - 1.2 µm) Location Body surface Deeper tissues Conduction velocity Very rapid (~12- 35 m/s) Very slow (~ 0.5 - 2 m/s) Neurotransmitter Glutamate (Option B) Substance P (Option A Ruled out) Description Rapid response Mediates the discriminative aspects of pain (localisation and intensity) Delayed, dull, intense, diffuse and unpleasant feeling associated with noxious stimulus

questions.question: Which type of receptor is known for its rapid adaptation to stimuli, making it particularly effective at detecting vibrations and rapid changes in pressure?

explanation.text: Pacinian receptors are rapidly adapting receptors sensitive to vibrations and rapid pressure changes Adaptation of receptors: One of the most important characteristics of sensory receptors is that they can adapt partially or completely to any constant stimulus after a period of time. When a continuous stimulus is applied to a

receptor, the initial response occurs at a high impulse rate, then at a progressively slower rate, which ultimately decreases to very few or none at all. Mechanism: Adaptation occurs in 2 ways: 1 In Rapidly Adapting Receptors It is a faster mechanism.

The receptors are viscoelastic in nature so that when a stimulus is applied to one side of the receptor, it is transmitted instantly by the viscous component to the same side of the central nerve fiber, eliciting a response Within a few seconds, the fluid in the receptors redistributes and the response is no longer elicited 2 In Slowly Adapting Receptors It is a slower mechanism called accommodation This occurs directly in the nerve fiber.
If there is a continued stimulus, then the tip of the receptor becomes accommodated to the stimulus. This occurs from the progressive inactivation of sodium channels in the nerve fiber membrane.

Rapidly adapting receptors Pacinian, Meissner’s and hearing organ Slow adapting receptors Merkel’s, Ruffini’s and free nerve endings (Option A & C ruled out) Meissner’s corpuscles (Option B) are also rapidly adapting receptors but are sensitive to light touch rather than vibrations.

questions.question: A researcher is studying various sensory receptors and their responses to different stimuli. During an experiment with pacinian corpuscle, the researcher notes that the intensity of the initial electrical response in the receptor is proportionate with the mechanical pressure applied. What is the initial graded electrical response observed in sensory receptors upon stimulus application?

explanation.text: Receptor potential is the graded depolarizing potential in a sensory receptor in response to a stimulus. Its magnitude varies with the intensity of the stimulus. Receptor Potentials A receptor potential is a type of graded potential that occurs in sensory receptors. It is a local, non-propagated change in membrane potential that occurs in response to a stimulus.

Receptor potential is not an action potential; instead, it causes the sensory neuron to fire action potentials. Once the receptor potential reaches a critical threshold, it triggers an action potential at the sensory nerve's first node of Ranvier. Factors affecting receptor potential: Proportional Response: Amplitude of receptor potential is generally proportional to stimulus intensity.

Nature: Non-propagated, depolarizing potential in sensory receptors. Threshold: When it reaches a critical level, an action potential is generated. Stimulus Intensity: Stronger stimuli lead to larger receptor potentials. Mechanism of receptor potential generation in Pacinian Corpuscle Pacinian Corpuscle Mechanism Mechanical Stimulation Pressure deforms lamellae surrounding sensory nerve ending.

Ion Channels Deformation opens mechanically-gated ion channels, mainly sodium (Na+). Sodium Influx Rapid influx of Na+ generates the receptor potential. Graded Response Larger deformation (stronger stimulus) leads to a larger receptor potential.

Action Potential If the potential reaches ~10 mV, an action potential is generated at the first Node of Ranvier. sensory Action potential (Option A) is an all-or-none electrical signal that occurs after the receptor potential reaches a threshold.
**Synaptic potential (Option C):** occurs at synapses between neurons, not in sensory receptors.
**Resting potential (Option D):** is the baseline electrical state of a cell when it is not stimulated.

questions.question: Which type of mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for two-point discrimination and the ability to read Braille by detecting fine touch and texture details on the fingertips?

explanation.text: Merkel discs are often grouped together in a receptor organ called touch domes, which project upward against the underside of the epithelium of the skin. This upward projection causes the epithelium to protrude, forming a dome (Iggo dome receptor, named after a scientist, Iggo) and creating an extremely sensitive receptor.
Blind individuals rely on the fine tactile acuity (two-point discrimination) of their fingertips to read Braille, which has dots spaced 2.5 mm apart.

**Rapidly Adapting Tactile Receptors Location Function Response Merkel’s Disc (Option C ruled out):** Underneath the epithelium of the skin Detect continuous touch and pressure, Transmit strong initial signal and weaker sustained signal, Localise touch sensations (Two point discrimination), Determine texture Transmit initially a strong response but partially adapting, then a continuing weaker response that adapts slowly.

**Extremely sensitive when grouped in a receptor organ called touch domes Ruffini Corpuscles (Option D ruled out):** Deeper layers of the skin and deeper internal tissues, joint capsules Important for signaling continuous states of deformation of tissue such as heavy prolonged touch and pressure Help to signal the degree of joint rotation Very slow adapting, providing continuous feedback about deformation and prolonged pressure.

**Free Nerve Ending (Option A ruled out):** Found everywhere in skin Detect touch and pressure Can detect even light contact Hair End Organ (Option B) detects movement of objects on the body surface or initial contact with the body

questions.question: Which type of receptor is most likely responsible for detecting the rapid changes in pressure and vibrations in the patient's fingertips?

explanation.text: Pacinian Corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors that are particularly sensitive to rapid changes in pressure and vibrations of tissues.

**Rapidly Adapting Tactile Receptors Structure Function Location Adaptation Pacinian Corpuscle (Option B):** Encapsulated nerve ending Detect tissue vibration or other rapid changes in the mechanical state of tissues Stimulated by rapid local compression of the tissue Immediately beneath the skin and deep in the fascial tissues of the body Adapts in a few hundredths of a second Meissner Corpuscle (Option A ruled

out) Elongated, encapsulated nerve ending of a large myelinated sensory nerve fiber Sensitive to movement of objects over the skin and low-frequency vibrations crucial for spatial location discernment of touch sensations Non-hairy skin, particularly abundant in fingertips and lips.

**Adapts in a fraction of a second Hair End Organ (Option C ruled out):** Nerve fiber entwined at the base of each hair Detects: Movement of objects on the body surface or Initial contact with the body Hairy skin Adapts readily

questions.question: A patient reports an unusual sensitivity to temperature changes, and you suspect a disorder related to thermoreceptor function. Which of the following statements accurately describes the nerve fibers involved in transmitting signals from thermoreceptors?

options.A: Cold receptors: myelinated type C fibers
options.B: Warmth receptors: myelinated type Aδ fibers
options.C: Cold receptors: myelinated type Aδ fibers
options.D: Warmth receptors: myelinated type Aβ fibers

explanation.text: Cold receptors primarily use small, myelinated type Aδ fibers to transmit signals, which conduct at a speed of approximately 20 m/sec.

**Types of Thermoreceptors Type Location Transmission Pathway Speed Cold Receptors (Option C):** Under the skin at spots Type Aδ fibers (myelinated), some Type C fibers (unmyelinated) (Option A ruled out) ~20 m/sec (Aδ fibers) Warmth Receptors (Option B&D Ruled out) Under the skin at spots Unmyelinated Type C fibers 0.4-2 m/sec The body has 3 - 10 times more cold spots (lips >>fingers) than warmth spots Nocireceptors / Pain receptors are stimulated only in extreme degrees of cold or heat and are responsible along with the cold and warmth receptors for freezing cold and burning hot sensations. Stimulation of Thermal Receptors Type of Nerve Fiber Temperature Range Cold Receptors 10-40°C (peak ~24°C) Warmth Receptors >30°C (fade ~49°C) Cold Pain Fibers Very cold temperatures Heat Pain Fibers Start ~45°C Thermal Signal Pathway Transmitted in parallel pathways with pain signals. Signals travel in the tract of Lissauer and terminate in laminae I, II, and III of dorsal horns. Processed signals by cord neurons cross to the opposite anterolateral sensory tract and terminate in both brain stem's reticular areas and the thalamus's ventrobasal complex. Removal of cortical postcentral gyrus reduces, but does not eliminate, temperature distinction ability.

questions.question: Which layer of the cerebral cortex is primarily responsible for receiving input sensory signals and sending them to other layers?

explanation.text: Layer IV is the primary input layer where sensory signals first enter the cortex. It processes these signals and then distributes them to other layers. Cerebral Cortex Layers and Functions: Has six layers of neurons. Layer Function I- Molecular layer Receives nonspecific input signals from lower brain centers. Control the excitability of stimulated areas.

II- External granular layer Receives nonspecific input and sends axons to the opposite cortex through the corpus callosum. III- External pyramidal layer Sends axons to related cortical areas on the opposite side through the corpus callosum. IV- Internal granular layer The primary layer for receiving input sensory signals, which then spread to the surface and deeper layers.

V- Internal pyramidal layer Sends large axons to distant nervous system parts like basal ganglia, brain stem, and spinal cord. Controls signal transmission. VI- Fusiform/ polymorphic layer Sends axons to the thalamus. Regulates excitability of incoming sensory signals.

questions.question: A patient presents to the clinic with difficulty feeling the precise location of a stimulus on their skin and reports problems distinguishing between different textures and shapes. Additionally, they are having trouble detecting rapid changes in vibrations. Which of the following somatosensory pathways is most likely affected in this patient, given their symptoms?

explanation.text: The Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscal System handles precise touch localization, texture, vibration, and proprioception. The patient’s difficulty with these sensations suggests an issue with this system. Somatosensory pathways: Two primary somatosensory pathways that transmit sensory signals from the body to the brain: the dorsal column-medial lemniscal system and the anterolateral system.

**Pathway Sensory Modalities Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscal System (Option A):** Touch: Provides precise localization and fine gradations of intensity. Vibration: Detects rapid changes in stimulus through phasic sensations. Proprioception: Contributes to the sense of body position and movement. Pressure: Allows for the perception of fine degrees of pressure intensity. Anterolateral System (Option B & C) Lateral Spinothalamic Tract: Transmits sensations of pain and temperature (warmth and cold). Anterior Spinothalamic Tract: Carries crude touch and pressure for general skin contact, along with tickle, itch, and sexual sensations. Corticospinal Tract is involved in motor control, not sensory discrimination. (Option D)

questions.question: A 45 Y/o man presents with numbness and loss of proprioception in his right leg and lower torso. Upon examination, the physician notes a loss of vibration sense and two-point discrimination in the affected areas. MRI shows a lesion in the medulla. Which of the following nucleus is most likely affected?

explanation.text: Based on the above scenario, the patient is most likely having a lesion in the Nucleus gracilis Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway: Pathway Sensory receptors → Spinal cord (dorsal roots) → Brain (somatosensory cortex) Neurons First-order neurons Originate in mechanoreceptors, and enter spinal cord via dorsal roots Pseudo-unipolar neurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion Split into medial and lateral

branches: Medial branch: Travels up dorsal column to brain Lateral branch: Synapses in dorsal horn, forming local reflexes, spinocerebellar tracts Fibers from lower thoracic, sacral, and lumbar regions (T7-T12, L, S) ascend to medulla without synapsing, forming the fasciculus gracilis Fibers from cervical and upper thoracic regions (C, T1-T6) ascend to medulla without synapsing, forming the fasciculus cuneatus Second-order neurons Synapse in dorsal medulla (cuneate nucleus for upper body, gracile nucleus for lower body) Cross to opposite brain stem side, travel to thalamus (medial lemniscus) Third-order neurons Synapse in thalamus (ventrobasal complex) Project to somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, lateral parietal cortex) Nucleus cuneatus: Transmits sensory information from the upper body (arms and upper torso).

The patient's symptoms do not involve these areas. (Option A) Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL): Located in the thalamus, not the medulla. This option is incorrect because the lesion is in the medulla. (Option C) Nucleus ambiguus: Involved in motor control of the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles. It is not related to the dorsal column pathway or the sensory symptoms described. (Option D)

questions.question: A patient presents with a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of the body, below the level of a spinal cord lesion. Upon examination, the patient also exhibits impaired sensation of crude touch and itch on the same side but fine touch and proprioception sensations are intact. Which sensory pathway is most likely affected in this patient?

explanation.text: Based on the above scenario, the patient most likely has a lesion in the anterolateral pathway.. Anterolateral Pathway Transmits sensory signals such as pain, temperature, crude touch, itch, sexual sensations, and crude pressure from the opposite side of the body. Damage results in loss of pain and temperature sensation on the opposite side below the lesion.

Characteristics: Slower transmission, less precise spatial localization, reduced ability to transmit rapidly changing signals. Pathway: Origin and Path Sensory signals enter the spinal cord via dorsal roots; and originate from nociceptors, thermoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors. First Order Neurons Afferent fibers with cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG); terminate in the dorsal horn.

Second Order Neurons Cell bodies in laminae I, II, and V of the dorsal horn; axons cross the midline and ascend in the anterolateral funiculus. Synapses with VPL of the thalamus Crude Touch Fibers -Form the anterior spinothalamic tract. Pain and Temperature Fibers - Form the lateral spinothalamic tract. Third Order Neurons Originate from VPL, midline, and intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus; project to specific sensory cortex areas.
Termination Points Reticular nuclei of the brainstem; Thalamus: Ventrobasal complex (tactile signals) and intralaminar nuclei (pain signals).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the sensory and motor deficits in Brown-Séquard Syndrome?

options.A: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature; ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration.
options.B: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature; contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration.
options.C: Ipsilateral loss of all sensations at the lesion; contralateral motor loss below the lesion.
options.D: Contralateral loss of vibration and fine touch; ipsilateral loss of temperature, and crude touch.

explanation.text: Spinal cord syndromes: Condition Description Clinical Findings Brown-Séquard Syndrome Hemisection of the spinal cord.

Ipsilateral loss of all sensation at the level of the lesion; ipsilateral LMN signs (e.g., flaccid paralysis) at the level of the lesion; Ipsilateral UMN signs below the level of lesion (due to corticospinal tract damage); Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch below the level of lesion (due to dorsal column damage); Contralateral loss of pain, temperature, and crude touch below the level of lesion (due to spinothalamic tract damage); If a lesion occurs above T1, it may present with ipsilateral Horner syndrome due to damage of the oculosympathetic pathway.

Anterior Spinal Artery Occlusion Spinal cord infarction sparing dorsal horns and columns. Watershed area mid-thoracic; Artery of Adamkiewicz supplies ASA below T8. Can follow aortic aneurysm repair. Presents with UMN signs below lesion (corticospinal tract), LMN signs at the level of lesion (anterior horn), and Loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion (spinothalamic tract).

Tabes Dorsalis Degeneration/demyelination of dorsal columns and roots caused by Treponema pallidum (tertiary syphilis). Progressive sensory ataxia (impaired proprioception and poor coordination); Positive Romberg sign; Absent deep tendon reflexes (DTRs); Seen in the terminal stage of syphilis Associated with shooting pain, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints.

Syringomyelia A fluid-filled, gliosis-lined cavity within the spinal cord, Often associated with Chiari I malformation. “Cape-like” loss of pain and temperature sensation in bilateral upper extremities (due to damage of fibers crossing in anterior white commissure); LMN deficits if anterior horns are affected; Most lesions occur between C2 and T9.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding removal of each somatosensory area is correct?

options.A: Somatosensory Area I: complete loss of pain and temperature sensations.
options.B: Somatosensory Area II: inability of precise localization of sensations
options.C: Somatosensory Association Areas: inability to recognize two sides of an object
options.D: Somatosensory Area I: enhance ability to judge the shape of an object

explanation.text: Feature Somatosensory Area I (SSA 1) Somatosensory Area II (SSA 2) Somatosensory Association Area Location Postcentral gyrus (Brodmann's areas 3, 1, and 2). Superior wall of Sylvian fissure Brodmann's areas 5 and 7, located in parietal cortex behind SSA I Representation and localisation High localization of body parts.

Nose, lips, mouth and face laterally; head, neck, shoulder and lower body part medially Poor localization (Option B) Face is represented anteriorly, arms centrally and legs posteriorly Combines information from the primary somatosensory area, leading to complex sensations, such as feeling an object like a knife or ball.

Function Primary area for somatic sensation Less known functions; Relies on input from SSA I Decipher deeper meanings of sensory information from SSA Sensory Information Receive inputs from thalamic and cortical areas Signals enter from brain stem, SSA I and from other sensory areas (visual and auditory) Receives signals from SSA I, thalamus,visual cortex and auditory cortex Effect of Excision B/L excision of leads to: Loss of precise localization of sensations Inability to judge pressure against the body, weight, texture, or shape of the object (astereognosis) (Option D).

**Pain and temperature senses preserved but poorly localized (Option A):** Removal of parts of SSA II does not affect the response of neurons in SSA I U/L removal leads to: Amorphosynthesis: Difficulty recognizing objects on one side. (Option C) Hemineglect: Denial of the existence of the opposite side of the body. Constructional apraxia: Difficulty in constructing a picture.

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately describes the representation in motor and sensory homunculus?

options.A: Hand and digits have large cortical representation in the motor homunculus
options.B: Feet represented at the bottom of both the precentral gyrus and postcentral gyrus
options.C: Trunk and back have large cortical representation in both homunculi
options.D: Cortical representation is proportional to the size of the body part in both homunculi

explanation.text: Homunculus represents either the motor or the sensory distribution along the cerebral cortex of the brain.

Feature Motor Homunculus Sensory Homunculus Location Precentral gyrus Postcentral gyrus Representation Feet at the top of the gyrus (Option B); face at the bottom Legs on top and head at the bottom of the gyrus (Option B) Cortical Representation (Option D) Proportionate to the skill involved in fine, voluntary activities Proportional to the number of sensory receptors that sense muscle position and changes in muscle length Large Representation Areas (Option C) Hand, digits (Option A), lips, jaw, and tongue (areas involved in speech and hand movements) Face (especially lips), Hand (especially digits) (Option A) Small Representation Areas Trunk and lower limb Trunk and lower limb Specialization Large area for lips, jaw, and tongue due to specialization in speech (vocalization of the cortex) Large area for face mainly lips) due to speech Large area for hand(mainly digits) due to cutaneous sensations from areas involved in skilled activities Sensory Homunculus: Motor Homunculus:

questions.question: A 45-year-old man recently had his right leg amputated below the knee. Weeks after surgery, he feels sensations and pain in the missing leg area, sometimes triggered by touching his thigh. Which statement best explains the patient's condition and suggests a treatment?

options.A: Brain reorganization of cortical brain area & Spinal cord stimulation may help.
options.B: Infection at the amputation site causes pain & Antibiotics should be prescribed.
options.C: Reorganization at spinal cord neuronal connection leading to pain.
options.D: Pain is due to rejection of the prosthetic limb & Discontinue use immediately.

explanation.text: Cortical plasticity Refers to the ability of neurons to modify their connections under specific circumstances. Cortical structures are capable of reorganization (plasticity) after loss of a body part, neighboring areas take over the cortical area of the lost part. (Option A). Cortical connections of sensory units become weak with disuse and strengthen with use.

Phantom Limb Pain Perceived due to cortical plasticity In the phantom limb phenomenon, the limb actually does not exist (amputated), but the patient complains that he feels pain or itch in the limb Based on the evidence, brain reorganization occurs when sensory input is cut off.

For example: In leg amputees, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus can perceive the signal that once received input from leg and foot now responds to stump (thigh) stimulation Management: Epidural Anesthesia: Used during amputation surgery to reduce acute pain and subsequent need for opioids, lowering phantom pain incidence.
Spinal Cord Stimulation: Electric current stimulates spinal pathways, reducing phantom limb pain and causing a tingling sensation instead in phantom limb (Option A)

questions.question: Which law explains the phenomenon of phantom limb pain?

options.A: Muller's Doctrine of Specific Nerve Energy

explanation.text: The law of Projection forms the basis of phantom limb Laws of Sensory Physiology Bell-Magendie Law: States that the dorsal root of the spinal cord is sensory and the ventral root of the spinal cord is motor in function. (Option B) Muller's Doctrine of Specific Nerve Energy: States that sensation evoked by a stimulus that generates impulse in the specific sensory pathway depends on the precise area of the brain that is eventually activated by the stimulus. (Option A) Law of Projection: States that no matter where a specific sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the sensation is referred to the location of the receptors.

Forms the basis of the phantom limb. (Option C) Weber-Fechner Law: States that the magnitude of sensation felt is proportionate to the logarithm of the intensity of the stimulus. (Option D) Interpreted signal strength = Log (Stimulus) + Constant Emphasizes that the greater the background sensory intensity, the greater an additional change must be for the individual to detect the change.
Labelled Line Theory States that each sensory receptor is specialized to detect specific stimuli and sends signals via dedicated nerve fibers to the corresponding area of the somatosensory cortex.

questions.question: A 45 Y/o right-handed woman presents with difficulty in performing coordinated movements and a lack of fluidity in her actions, particularly when performing tasks that require the integration of both hands, such as typing or playing the piano. Which of the following brain regions is most likely implicated in her condition?

explanation.text: Based on the above scenario, the patient most likely has a lesion in the supplementary motor cortex, which is important for complex bimanual coordination. Cortical Motor areas: The motor cortex is located in the frontal lobe.

Primary Motor Cortex: Corresponds to Brodmann Area 4 It lies in the first convolution of the frontal lobes anterior to the central sulcus Responsible for executing voluntary movements and controlling fine motor skills (Option A) Premotor Cortex: Corresponds to Brodmann area 6 Lies 1-3 cm anterior to the primary motor area Responsible for setting posture before movement (Option B) Supplementary Motor Cortex: Lies mainly in the longitudinal fissure Responsible for Bimanual coordination (Option C) Cortical Association Areas: Commands for voluntary movements originate in cortical association areas (Option D)

questions.question: Which of the following is the major contributor to the corticospinal tract in terms of percentage of descending fibers?

explanation.text: Corticospinal tract: The corticospinal tract, also known as the pyramidal tract, is the most important descending tract from the motor cortex. Contribution: Primary motor cortex- 30% (Option A) Premotor and supplementary cortex- 30% (Options B&C) Somatosensory area- 40% (Option D) After leaving the cortex, the tract passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, then through the brainstem and into the medulla.

In the medulla, most of the fibers cross to the opposite side, forming the medullary pyramids. These crossed fibers descend as the lateral corticospinal tract finally terminates in the spinal cord. Some fibers which do not cross to the opposite side in the medulla pass ipsilaterally down to the spinal cord as the ventral corticospinal tract.
